analysis.one_liner: Caps pain-and-suffering awards in medical malpractice lawsuits at $250,000 and tightens expert-witness rules.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Sen. Jon Kyl with one cosponsor in September 2009, was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the rules for medical malpractice lawsuits nationwide. It would have kept unlimited compensation for measurable losses like medical bills and lost wages, but capped awards for pain, suffering, disfigurement, and loss of companionship at $250,000 per provider, with a $500,000 ceiling when multiple institutions are liable. It would also have required injured patients to submit a preliminary expert affidavit early in their case or have it dismissed, set strict qualifications for expert witnesses, and overridden state laws that allow larger awards.
analysis.who_benefits: Physicians, hospitals, and medical malpractice insurers would gain the most. Capping the unpredictable noneconomic damages that drive verdicts and insurance premiums would shield providers from large jury awards and lower malpractice insurance costs, as the bill's own findings argue happened in Texas after its 2003 cap.

how_it_helps.text: Caps noneconomic damages at $250,000 from any single provider or institution, and $500,000 total from multiple institutions, limiting the largest jury awards against health care providers.
Leaves economic damages like medical bills and lost earnings uncapped, so patients can still recover their verifiable financial losses in full.
Adopts a fair-share rule so each defendant pays only its own percentage of responsibility, ending joint liability where a largely blameless deep-pocketed defendant covers others' shares.

Requires claimants to certify whether expert testimony is needed and serve a preliminary expert opinion affidavit, with dismissal if they fail to, and bars experts whose fees depend on the outcome, which the bill's findings describe as deterring weak lawsuits.

analysis.who_pays: Patients seriously injured by medical negligence. People whose losses are mostly intangible — a child killed by malpractice, a permanently disfigured or disabled patient, a homemaker with no lost wages — would see their compensation capped at $250,000 regardless of how severe the injury or how clear the negligence. Stricter filing requirements would also add hurdles for malpractice victims suing large institutions with far greater legal resources.

drawbacks.text: The cap falls hardest on patients with severe, life-altering injuries whose damages are largely noneconomic — pain, disability, disfigurement, loss of a loved one — since they would be limited to $250,000 no matter what a jury found their suffering was worth.
The bill preempts state laws that allow larger awards, overriding states that have chosen higher caps or no caps at all, despite the bill's own section titled 'protection of states' rights.'

The early expert-affidavit requirement would add cost and procedural risk for malpractice victims, whose cases are expensive to bring and who typically face well-funded hospital and insurer defense teams.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real argument for the bill: frivolous suits and defensive medicine add cost to health care, and the bill cites CBO estimates of roughly $5.6 billion in direct federal savings from similar reforms [S3]. But the savings come almost entirely out of the pockets of the most severely injured patients, whose compensation would be capped at the same $250,000 whether their injury was moderate or catastrophic. The bill also preempts state law, cutting against its states'-rights framing. On balance it shifts money from injured patients to providers and insurers, with uncertain, debated savings for everyone else.

outcome.mechanism: Kyl introduced it at the end of September 2009, the Senate sent it to the Judiciary Committee, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Sen. Jon Kyl introduced the Medical Liability Reform Act of 2009 in the Senate on September 30, 2009, with Sen. John Cornyn as the other original sponsor.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day; that referral was the only committee action in its entire history.
The bill attracted just one cosponsor besides its original sponsors, and the Judiciary Committee never scheduled a hearing or vote before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Patients injured by medical negligence, and the plaintiffs' bar that represents them, are better off that the bill never became law, since it would have capped their recoveries. Supporters of malpractice caps lost a legislative opportunity, though the bill was so lightly supported it was unlikely to advance.

for.name: Sen. Jon Kyl
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its lead sponsor.

for.name: Sen. John Cornyn
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's co-sponsor at introduction.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Sen. Patrick Leahy (D-VT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on September 30, 2009 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced and cosponsored solely by Republicans — two original sponsors and one additional cosponsor among the 40 Senate Republicans — with no Democratic support, and the Democratic-run Judiciary Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: Caps on noneconomic damages directly limit the payouts insurers must make on malpractice claims. The bill's findings tout Texas premium declines of 27% after its 2003 cap [S3]; insurers' gain comes at the cost of reduced compensation for injured patients.

Providers would face predictable, capped exposure instead of open-ended jury awards, and fewer weak suits under the affidavit requirement. The benefit to patients through lower costs and better access, as claimed in the bill's findings, is contested and would come partly at injured patients' expense.
Contingency-fee lawyers and their clients would see case values slashed by the caps and cases dismissed for missing early expert affidavits, shrinking the market for malpractice litigation.
